reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: Typically affects children, adolescents, and young adults, with a peak in the second decade and a modest male predominance
Classically arises in the diaphysis or metadiaphysis of long bones and in the flat bones of the pelvis, although extraskeletal soft-tissue forms occur
Presents with localised pain and swelling that may mimic osteomyelitis, sometimes with fever, raised inflammatory markers, and a lamellated (onion-skin) periosteal reaction on plain films
Histologically a small round blue cell tumour with strong, diffuse membranous CD99 (MIC2) expression, though CD99 is not specific and must be interpreted with molecular confirmation
Defined by recurrent FET-ETS gene fusions, most commonly EWSR1-FLI1 from a t(11;22) translocation, with EWSR1-ERG the next most frequent
Multimodality care combines multi-agent chemotherapy with local control by surgery, radiotherapy, or both, reflecting inherent chemo- and radiosensitivity
Around a fifth to a quarter of patients have overt metastatic disease at diagnosis, most often to lung, bone, and marrow, which strongly influences outcome
Staging must include cross-sectional imaging of the primary, chest CT, whole-body assessment, and bone-marrow evaluation before treatment begins
reference.pathophysiology: Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive small round cell malignancy driven by a chimeric transcription factor produced when a FET-family gene (usually EWSR1) fuses with an ETS-family partner (most often FLI1, less commonly ERG). The resulting fusion protein acts as an aberrant transcription factor that reprogrammes gene expression, binds GGAA microsatellite repeats to switch on oncogenic targets, and blocks the differentiation of a permissive mesenchymal or neural crest-like progenitor cell. This single dominant genetic event, occurring against an otherwise quiet genome, sustains uncontrolled proliferation and impaired maturation, and its detection underpins molecular diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Rhabdomyosarcoma and other small round cell tumours
CIC-rearranged and BCOR-altered undifferentiated round cell sarcomas
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the entire involved bone and adjacent soft tissue to define local extent and skip lesions
Plain radiographs to characterise the permeative lytic pattern and periosteal reaction
Chest CT to detect pulmonary metastases
Whole-body staging with functional imaging and skeletal survey to identify distant bony disease
Bone-marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude marrow involvement
Image-guided or open biopsy with molecular testing (FISH or RT-PCR) for EWSR1 rearrangement and immunohistochemistry including CD99 and NKX2.2
redFlags: A destructive bone lesion with a soft-tissue mass in a child or young adult, mistaken for infection and treated with antibiotics alone
Systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and raised inflammatory markers accompanying a bone lesion
Rapidly enlarging mass, pathological fracture, or neurological compromise from spinal or paraspinal disease
Symptoms of widespread disease (bone pain, cytopenias) suggesting marrow or multifocal involvement
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on stage, primary site, tumour volume, and response to induction chemotherapy; patients with localised, resectable disease that responds well have markedly better survival than those with metastatic disease at presentation, particularly bone or marrow metastases, which carry a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Attributing the presentation to osteomyelitis and delaying biopsy and imaging
Placing the biopsy tract without discussion with the treating surgeon, potentially compromising later limb-sparing resection
Relying on CD99 positivity alone, since it is shared by lymphoblastic and other tumours, without molecular confirmation
Omitting bone-marrow evaluation and thereby understaging the disease
Underestimating late effects of therapy, including second malignancies and treatment-related toxicity in long-term survivors
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Neoadjuvant multi-agent chemotherapy exploiting inherent chemosensitivity, typically vincristine, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide alternating with ifosfamide and etoposide
Local control after induction with wide surgical resection, radiotherapy, or both depending on site and resectability
Adjuvant chemotherapy to consolidate response and treat micrometastatic disease
Radiotherapy for unresectable primaries or positive margins, reflecting the tumour's radiosensitivity
Supportive oncology care: growth-factor and antiemetic support, neutropenic-sepsis management and fertility preservation before treatment
Surveillance for local recurrence and pulmonary metastases and monitoring for late effects such as anthracycline cardiotoxicity and second malignancy
Management within a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team
